name: The Turning Stair
goal: Repeat work with loops, and choose between counting, accumulating and searching.

description.what: The two ways Python repeats work - `while`, which keeps going until a condition stops holding, and `for`, which visits each thing in turn - together with `range` and the three jobs that nearly every loop you will ever write is doing.
description.why: Without repetition a program can only be as long as the work it does, so a hundred readings would mean a hundred lines and a million would be impossible; a loop is what lets four lines of source handle an amount of work you did not know in advance.
description.enables: You will be able to keep a program going until something becomes true, visit every character of a piece of text or every number in a counted span, and build a running total, a running count or a first-match answer as you go.
description.assumes: You can store a value under a name and change what it refers to, work out an expression by hand, and write an `if` whose condition is either True or False. Nothing about functions, lists or text methods is needed.
description.assessed: You will predict what loops print, trace a running value pass by pass, repair a loop that stops one pass too early, and write whole programs for problems where nobody tells you which of the three patterns is wanted.

sections.title: `while` - keep going until
sections.body:
A **loop** is an instruction that runs the same block of lines more than once. The first kind, `while`, reads almost as plain English: while this condition holds, do the block again. Python checks the condition, runs the block if it is True, then goes back and checks again - and only when the check comes out False does it move on to the line after the loop.

The shape is the shape you already know from `if`: a header line ending in a colon, then an indented block. The indentation is what says which lines belong to the loop; the first line back at the outer level is the first line that runs after it.

Everything hangs on one thing, and it is the thing beginners forget: **something inside the block must change what the condition asks about**. If the block never touches `count`, then `count > 0` is True on the first check and True on every check after it, and the program runs the block forever. That is an **infinite loop**, and the way you spot one is by asking, of every `while` you write, which line makes the condition eventually go False.

Use `while` when you do not know in advance how many passes there will be - keep asking until the answer is right, keep reading until the word `stop` arrives, keep halving until the number reaches 1.
sections.code:
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("go")

annotations.text: The condition is checked BEFORE each pass. If `count` had started at 0 the block would never run even once.
This is the line that makes the loop end. Delete it and the program prints 3 forever.
Back at the outer indentation, so this runs once, after the loop has finished - not once per pass.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line.
checkpoint.code:
n = 1
while n < 20:
    print(n)
    n = n * 3
checkpoint.explain: The check happens before each pass, so 9 is printed and only then does 27 fail the test - 27 is never printed even though it is the value `n` ends up holding. Expecting a fourth line of 27 means you are picturing the condition being checked after the block rather than before it.

sections.title: `for` and `range` - do this to each
sections.body:
The second kind of loop, `for`, does not ask a question. It is handed a sequence of things and runs its block once for each of them, putting the current one under a name you choose. When it reaches the end of the sequence it stops, so a `for` loop over a finite sequence cannot run forever.

The commonest sequence to hand it is `range`, which produces a run of whole numbers. `range(3)` gives 0, 1, 2. `range(2, 5)` gives 2, 3, 4. A third argument is the step, and it may be negative: `range(10, 0, -4)` gives 10, 6, 2.

Now the detail that causes more beginner bugs than any other single thing in Python: **the stop value is not included**. `range(2, 5)` stops before 5, and this is called a **half-open** interval. It is why `range(5)` gives you exactly five numbers, and why `range(1, n)` visits every number from 1 up to but not including `n` - so to visit 1 to `n` inclusive you must write `range(1, n + 1)`.

A `for` loop also walks straight over a piece of text, one character at a time, in order. Use `for` when you know what you are visiting; use `while` when you know only when to stop.

annotations.text: One argument means start at 0. Three passes: `i` refers to 0, then 1, then 2.
Two arguments are start and stop. 2, 3, 4 - the stop value 5 never appears.
Three arguments add a step. Counting down: 10, 6, 2, and it stops before 0.
Text is a sequence of characters, so this runs three times with `letter` referring to `c`, then `a`, then `t`.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line.
checkpoint.code:
for i in range(1, 4):
    print(i * i)
checkpoint.explain: There are three passes, not four, because the stop value 4 is excluded - so 16 never appears. Writing a fourth line is the exact mistake the half-open interval is designed to catch you out on, and it is worth feeling it here rather than in a program that quietly reports one item too many.

sections.title: The three jobs a loop is nearly always doing
sections.body:
Almost every loop a working programmer writes is one of three shapes, and recognising which one a problem wants is more than half of solving it.

**Accumulate.** Set a name to a starting value before the loop - usually 0 - and on each pass replace it with itself plus something. At the end it holds the total. The starting value matters: begin a total at 0, because 0 plus anything is that thing.

**Count.** The same shape, but you add 1 only when a condition holds, so the name ends up holding how many times that condition was true. A count is an accumulator that adds 1 instead of a value.

**Search.** Set a name to a value meaning **nothing found yet**, then on each pass check whether this is the thing you wanted, and if it is, record it. At the end the name either holds the answer or still holds the not-found value, and both are useful results.

All three share one rule that is easy to get wrong: **the name is set up before the loop, not inside it**. Put `total = 0` inside the block and it is reset to 0 on every pass, so at the end it holds only the last item rather than the sum of all of them.

annotations.text: Set up before the loop. Inside it, this line would wipe the total on every pass and the answer would be 4.
The accumulator step: read the old value, add to it, put the label back on the answer. Total after the loop is 10.
A counter starts at 0 too, and this one is asking a question of each character rather than adding it.
Add 1, not the item. `banana` holds three letter `a` characters, so this prints 3.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the two blanks so that this program prints `1` - the number of times the letter `o` appears in `storm`.
checkpoint.explain: A counter has to start at 0 because it must be correct for text containing no `o` at all, and it has to grow by 1 rather than by the letter, since you are counting occurrences and not adding up characters. Starting at 1 gives an answer that is one too high on every input, which is a bug that looks like an off-by-one but is really a set-up error.

sections.title: `break`, `continue`, and loops that never end
sections.body:
Two words change a loop's flow from inside its block. `break` abandons the loop entirely and the program carries on at the first line after it. `continue` abandons only the rest of this pass and goes straight to the next one.

`break` is what makes the deliberate infinite loop useful. `while True` has a condition that never goes False, so on its own it would run forever - but with a `break` inside, it becomes the natural way to say **keep going until something happens that I cannot test in advance**, such as a particular line being typed.

An accidental infinite loop looks the same and is a bug. The two questions that find one: does anything in the block change what the condition asks about, and does that change move the value towards making the condition False? A loop counting up while it waits for its value to drop below zero satisfies the first question and fails the second.

One warning about `break`, because it is a common confusion in the exam ahead: `break` and `continue` look similar and behave completely differently. Using `break` where you wanted `continue` does not skip one item, it throws away every item that was still to come.

annotations.text: Leaves the loop the instant `i` refers to 3, so this loop prints 0, 1, 2 and never sees 3 through 9.
Skips the rest of this pass only. The loop keeps running, so 2 is missing from the output but 3 and 4 still appear.
Not reached on the pass where `i` refers to 2, because `continue` jumped over it.

checkpoint.explain: `while True` never ends on its own, so the `break` is the only exit and the loop stops on the first `n` whose square passes 20 - that is 5, since 16 is not greater than 20 but 25 is. Answering 4 means you tested `n` itself against 20 rather than `n * n`.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line.
guided-practice.code:
steps = 0
while steps < 3:
    print("step", steps)
    steps = steps + 1
print("done", steps)
guided-practice.explain: The counter starts at 0 and the condition stops it at 3, so the loop runs three times and the numbers printed are 0, 1 and 2 - never 3. The final line is outside the loop and runs once, and it shows the value that failed the check, which is why `done 3` is right and `done 2` is the tempting wrong answer.
guided-practice.hint: Write down what `steps` refers to before each check of the condition, then say whether the block runs.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line.
guided-practice.code:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 6):
    total = total + i
    print(i, total)
guided-practice.explain: `range(1, 6)` gives five numbers because the stop value is excluded, and the running total is printed inside the loop, so there are five lines rather than one. Each line shows the total AFTER that number has been added, which is why the first line reads `1 1` and not `1 0`.
guided-practice.hint: Keep two columns on paper: the value of `i` on this pass, and the value of `total` after the addition.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the two blanks so this program prints `5`, `4`, `3`, `2`, `1` on five lines and then stops.
guided-practice.template:
n = 5
while n ___ 0:
    print(n)
    n = n ___ 1
guided-practice.explain: The condition must exclude 0 or a sixth line appears, and the block must move `n` downwards or the condition never goes False and the program never stops. Writing `>=` is the off-by-one here, and writing `+` is the infinite loop - the two commonest ways a countdown goes wrong.
guided-practice.hint: One blank decides where the countdown stops; the other decides whether it stops at all.

guided-practice.prompt: This loop builds a running total of square numbers. Give the value `total` refers to after each pass of the loop.

steps.label: after the pass where i is 1
after the pass where i is 2
after the pass where i is 3

guided-practice.explain: Each pass reads the old total and writes a new one, so the values grow 1, 5, 14 rather than being replaced by 1, 4, 9. If you wrote the squares themselves you traced the expression on the right of the `+` instead of the name on the left, which is exactly the confusion the accumulator pattern exists to make visible.
guided-practice.hint: On each pass work out `i * i` first, then add it to whatever `total` held a moment ago.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a program that reads one typed line holding a whole number `n`, and prints the sum of every whole number from 1 to `n` inclusive. For the typed line `5` it prints `15`, because 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 is 15. If `n` is 0 there is nothing to add and it prints `0`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
n = int(input())
total = 0
# Loop over the numbers 1 to n, adding each one to total.
# Then print total, once, after the loop has finished.
guided-practice.solution:
n = int(input())
total = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    total = total + i
print(total)
guided-practice.explain: This is the accumulator pattern with the half-open interval trap attached: `range(1, n)` would leave out `n` itself and every answer would be short by exactly `n`. The `0` test is the one that catches a `while` written with the check in the wrong place, because a loop that runs at least once before checking would print 1 there instead of 0.
guided-practice.hint: `range(1, n + 1)` is the span from 1 to `n` inclusive. Set `total` up before the loop and print it after.

guided-practice.prompt: This program should read one typed line holding a whole number `n` and print every whole number from 1 to `n` inclusive, one per line - so for the typed line `3` it prints `1`, `2`, `3`. Instead it always stops one number early, and for the typed line `1` it prints nothing at all. Repair it.
guided-practice.explain: `range` never produces its stop value, so `range(1, n)` covers 1 up to `n - 1` and the last number is silently lost. The `1` test is the one that makes the fault obvious rather than subtle: `range(1, 1)` is empty, so the whole program prints nothing, and a bug that produces no output at all is much easier to see than one that is quietly short by one.
guided-practice.hint: The loop is right about where to start and wrong about where to stop. Compare `range(1, 3)` with the numbers you were asked for.

independent-practice.prompt: The first typed line holds a whole number saying how many readings follow, and that many typed lines follow it, each holding one whole number. Print the largest of the readings. For the typed lines `3`, `4`, `9` and `2` the program prints `9`. There is always at least one reading.
independent-practice.solution:
count = int(input())
best = int(input())
seen = 1
while seen < count:
    value = int(input())
    if value > best:
        best = value
    seen = seen + 1
print(best)
independent-practice.explain: Starting the running best at 0 rather than at the first reading is the fault this problem is built to expose - the all-negative case then prints 0, a number that was never in the data at all. Reading the first value before the loop and comparing the rest against it is the only version that is right for every possible input.

independent-practice.prompt: Read one typed line of text and print how many of its characters are the letter `e`. For the typed line `sequence` it prints `3`. Text containing no `e` at all prints `0`.
independent-practice.explain: Text is a sequence, so a program can visit it character by character without knowing how long it is - which is what makes one program work for `xyz` and for a thousand-character line alike. The `Eel` test matters because a capital `E` is a different character from a lower-case one, so an answer of 2 there means you assumed a comparison ignores case when it does not.

independent-practice.prompt: The first typed line holds a word. Exactly five more typed lines follow it. Print the position of the first of those five lines that is equal to the word, counting the first of the five as position 1. If none of the five is equal to the word, print `0`. For the word `cat` followed by `dog`, `cat`, `owl`, `cat` and `bat`, the program prints `2`.

tests.input:
cat
dog
cat
owl
cat
bat

cat
a
b
c
d
e

cat
cat
cat
cat
cat
cat

cat
x
y
z
w
cat

independent-practice.solution:
word = input()
found = 0
place = 1
while place <= 5:
    line = input()
    if line == word and found == 0:
        found = place
    place = place + 1
print(found)
independent-practice.explain: The answer has to be the FIRST match, so a program that keeps overwriting its answer reports 4 instead of 2 on the worked example. Guarding the record with `found == 0`, or leaving the loop the moment a match appears, both fix it - and the not-found case is why the answer needs a starting value that could never be a real position.

independent-practice.prompt: Read one typed line holding a whole number of 1 or more. Print the smallest multiple of that number which is strictly greater than 100. For the typed line `7` it prints `105`. For the typed line `101` it prints `101`, since 101 is itself a multiple of 101 and is already past 100.
independent-practice.solution:
n = int(input())
value = n
while value <= 100:
    value = value + n
print(value)
independent-practice.explain: Nobody can say in advance how many steps this takes - one for 101, a hundred for 1 - so the number of passes has to be decided by the condition rather than counted out beforehand. The `100` test is the boundary: strictly greater means 100 itself is not an acceptable answer, and a condition written with `<` instead of `<=` prints it and is wrong by exactly that one case.

independent-practice.prompt: Typed lines arrive one at a time. Each line holds either a whole number or the word `stop`. Print the sum of the numbers that arrived before `stop`, and print it as soon as `stop` arrives - nothing after that line matters. For the typed lines `4`, `6` and `stop` the program prints `10`. If `stop` is the very first line it prints `0`.
independent-practice.solution:
total = 0
while True:
    line = input()
    if line == "stop":
        break
    total = total + int(line)
print(total)
independent-practice.explain: The number of lines is not known before the program runs and is not stated anywhere in the input, so the only thing that can end this loop is the arrival of the sentinel word itself. Converting every line to a number before checking it is the trap: `stop` is not a number, so that order of operations fails on the very line that is supposed to end the program cleanly.

exam.prompt: Which whole numbers does `range(2, 6)` produce, in order?
exam.explain: The first option is the tempting one because `2, 6` reads like from 2 to 6, and in ordinary English it would be. `range` is half-open: it starts at the first argument and stops BEFORE the second, which is what makes `range(0, 6)` hold exactly six numbers and is the source of nearly every off-by-one error on this floor.

exam.prompt: Select every statement that correctly describes `break` or `continue`.
choices: `break` ends the whole loop at once, and the program carries on at the first line after it
`continue` ends the whole loop at once, and the program carries on at the first line after it
`continue` abandons the rest of the current pass and goes straight on to the next pass
`break` abandons the rest of the current pass and goes straight on to the next pass
A `while True` loop needs a `break` inside it, because its condition never becomes False
exam.explain: The two wrong options are the definitions swapped over, which is exactly how this pair is misremembered: both words interrupt the block, and the difference is only whether the loop survives the interruption. Using `break` where `continue` was wanted does not skip one item, it discards every item still to come.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line.
exam.explain: 2 is skipped but the loop survives, so 3 still appears; 4 ends the loop outright, so 5 never gets a chance. Answering 0, 1, 3, 5 means you read `break` as another skip, and answering 0, 1 means you read `continue` as ending the loop - the output separates the two readings on purpose.

exam.code:
n = 20
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n = n - 6
    steps = steps + 1
print(n, steps)
exam.explain: The condition is only checked between passes, never in the middle of one, so the fourth pass runs in full and takes `n` past 1 and down to -4. Expecting `2 3` means you assumed the loop stops the instant the value becomes small enough, which no loop does - it stops at the next check.

exam.prompt: This program should print the position of the first letter `n` in the word `sand`, counting the first letter as position 1, so it must print `3`. Fill the two blanks.
exam.template:
position = 0
place = 1
for letter in "sand":
    if letter == "n" and position == 0:
        position = ___
    place = place ___ 1
print(position)
exam.explain: The recorded answer is the position counter, not the letter and not the loop variable, because what was asked for is where the match was rather than what it was. The counter has to advance on every pass including the matching one, which is why the second blank sits outside the `if`.

exam.prompt: Arrange these lines into a program that reads one typed word and prints how many of its letters are `a`.
exam.explain: The counter has to be set up after the input is read but before the loop begins: put it inside the block and it is wiped on every pass, and put the `print` inside the block and you get one line of output per letter instead of one answer. Indentation is the visible record of which lines belong to the loop.

exam.prompt: Give the value `value` refers to after each pass of this loop.
exam.explain: There is a fourth pass because 27 is still under 40, and that pass overshoots to 81 - a `while` never stops part-way through its block. Stopping your trace at 27 is the same misreading as expecting a loop to check its condition in the middle of a pass.

exam.prompt: A learner writes `for i in range(1, n)` meaning to visit every number from 1 to `n` inclusive, and every run comes out one item short. Explain what `range` really does with its second argument, why this mistake is so easy to make, and what the correct line is.
exam.explain: Naming the rule is not the same as being able to say why it exists: the stop value is excluded so that counting a span of `n` items from 0 needs no adjustment at all, and the price of that convenience is that an inclusive span needs `n + 1`. A learner who can only report the symptom will fix this bug once and then write it again next week.

exam.prompt: Write a program that reads one typed line holding a whole number of 1 or more, and prints how many times that number can be halved, using whole-number division, before it reaches 1. For the typed line `8` it prints `3`, because 8 halves to 4, then 2, then 1. For the typed line `1` it prints `0`.
exam.starterCode:
n = int(input())
# Count the halvings here, then print the count.
exam.solution:
n = int(input())
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n = n // 2
    steps = steps + 1
print(steps)
exam.explain: Nobody can say from the input how many passes this takes, so the count has to come out of the loop rather than being fixed before it - that is precisely the situation `while` exists for. The `1` test is the boundary that a loop checking its condition after the block would fail, printing 1 where the honest answer is 0 halvings.
exam.hint: A counter set up before the loop and increased once per pass is the whole answer.

exam.prompt: This program should read one typed line holding a whole number `n` and print how many of the numbers from 1 to `n` are not divisible by 3 - so for `7` it should print `5`, since 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 qualify. Instead it prints `2`. Repair it.
exam.starterCode:
n = int(input())
count = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    if i % 3 == 0:
        break
    count = count + 1
print(count)
exam.solution:
n = int(input())
count = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    if i % 3 == 0:
        continue
    count = count + 1
print(count)
exam.explain: `break` throws away every remaining number the moment the first multiple of 3 turns up, so the program really counts how many numbers come before the first multiple of 3 - which is why it answers 2 for every `n` of 3 or more. The `2` test is the one that hides the bug entirely, because no multiple of 3 is ever reached, and a test suite made only of small inputs would have shipped this.
exam.hint: One number should be skipped, not every number after it. Compare what the two loop-control words actually abandon.
